summary:
Open-loop sweep at 1a1c141, rates 8-128 req/s. At rate 128 the queue reached 2985 pending requests, and HALF the prefill waves were still K=1 (49%), with only 1% at K>=8. Max wave observed: 115 of a 256 batch. Demand was not the constraint — thousands of requests were waiting and the scheduler still prefilled one at a time.

Throughput plateaus accordingly: 163.9 tok/s at rate 8, then 612/620/782/665 for rates 16/32/64/128. Completed requests flatten at ~700-740 per 30s window = ~23-25 req/s capacity regardless of offered load. Offered load beyond ~16 req/s buys queue depth and latency, not work.

WHY IT MATTERS: decode is memory-bound — a step streams 9.2GB of dense weights whether it serves 1 sequence or 200. Roofline ceiling at B=256/L=512 is 31,268 tok/s; we measured ~780. Keeping the batch empty forfeits the single largest lever the hardware offers, and no kernel-level optimization can recover it.

This supersedes the earlier reading that 83-91% K=1 waves meant length-grouping was pointless: that was measured at low offered load where K=1 is CORRECT. At rate 128 it is not correct, and the cause is on the admission/wave path, not in the workload.
title: Prefill waves stay K=1 under overload — the batch never fills, and that is the bottleneck
triggers: a change that raises K>=8 share above ~20% at rate 128 would close this
measuring active_size during the window (not at the end) would localise it further
